newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles narrowly pass new constitution in referendum.
newsitem.headline: Poles narrowly pass new constitution in referendum.

text.p: In a nationwide referendum Poles narrowly approved a new constitution to replace the country's communist-era charter, official results released late on Monday showed.

PAP news agency quoted the State Election Commission as saying that of those taking part in the Sunday polls 52.71 percent backed the new constitution while 45.89 percent were opposed, with 1.40 percent of votes invalid. Out of 28.32 million eligible voters, 42.86 percent cast their vote.

The constitution, designed to enshrine Poland's democratic transformation since the 1989 fall of communism, was drafted by the ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and its Peasant allies together with two opposition parties in parliament.
It was passed by parliament on April 2 and will take effect in just over three months.
A "no" verdict would have left Poland with the remains of its discredited 1952 Stalinist constitution, amended by 1992 interim laws, until some future parliament could agree on a new version.
The constitution broadly retains the current political system while weakening the presidency. It sets caps on the government's spending but obliges it to support employment and home building.

It has been strongly criticised by Solidarity Electoral Action (AWS) -- an alliance of some 30 small right-wing parties clustered round the Solidarity trade union -- which hopes to win power in the September parliamentary polls.

The AWS, seeing Poland's history as bound up with the majority Roman Catholic faith, had wanted the charter to clearly invoke God, put religious values above man-made law and include a clause effectively banning abortion, now legal.
Catholic bishops, concerned over abortion, had also voiced deep moral reservations about the document.

The right wing also complained that a section of the new constitution allowing Poland to surrender by treaty some functions to international organisations -- to ease entry into European structures -- limited national sovereignty.
The constitution's authors said it made room for people of all faiths or none and, for example, left open the possibility of changing the abortion law by a future majority in parliament.
